reconcile.connective: JFB reads 'treat him as a publican' as borrowing a Jewish social convention for outsiders, not Jesus's own verdict on tax collectors.

discrepancy.connective: Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the plain conflict: the same Gospels that call Jesus a friend of publicans make 'publican' the model for someone to shun.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/publicans.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: Lastly, If even this fail, regard him as no longer a brother Christian, but as one "without"—as the Jews did Gentiles and publicans.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB glosses the 'treat him as a publican' clause as invoking the Jews' own customary treatment of outsiders, not Jesus's or the church's personal verdict on publicans as a class — directly addressing why the same Gospel can also call Jesus their friend.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871)
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats this exact passage directly, glossing Matthew 18:17's 'as a publican' clause as borrowing the Jews' own convention for treating outsiders rather than issuing a personal verdict on tax collectors. Haley's Alleged Discrepancies (1874) does not treat this pairing (verified via curl+grep of the full archive.org djvu text: no hit near 'heathen man' or Matthew 18; Haley's only 'publicans' discussion is a different discrepancy, Matt 21:31's 'publicans and harlots enter [the kingdom]' vs. texts excluding the impure).

link.title: Why does the Bible speak so negatively about tax collectors?
link.note: explains Matthew 18:17's 'treat him as a tax collector' as social separation aimed at evangelism, not contempt — resolving how Jesus could be 'a friend of publicans and sinners' while also instructing believers to distance from an unrepentant member
